Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
Going out at night or being outside after dark

issues.item: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
issues.explanation: These three maladaptive strategy items do not form a clinically coherent set on their own. 'Avoid Dreams' and 'Avoid Physical Stress' are trauma-linked avoidance strategies, but 'Compulsive Cleaning' reflects a distinct control/ritualising pattern that is not clearly tied to the same military PTSD presentation in the absence of any supporting trigger, threat, memory, or appraisal items. With no active edges in the formulation, the node should still be internally coherent; here the items suggest different mechanisms (nightmare avoidance, bodily arousal avoidance, and compulsive control rituals) without evidence they belong to the same symptom pattern.

vignette:
Nadia was 21 when she came to therapy, a single Middle Eastern woman working as a database administrator, and she spoke about the time after her deployment as if it had divided her life into before and after. The trauma had happened during a military convoy at dusk, when the light was already failing and the road ahead looked deceptively ordinary. She had been standing near an open vehicle door when a blast and the sudden chaos of shouting, smoke, and the metallic shock of bodies thrown out of order forced everything into a split second of helplessness. What stayed with her most was not only the violence of it, but how quickly the scene had turned from routine movement to a place where her body felt vulnerable and exposed. Since then, anything that reminded her of that bodily strain or of being out in the dark carried the force of that evening back with it.

In the months after returning home, Nadia began arranging her life around the feeling that if she could keep herself controlled and unburdened, she might keep danger at a distance. She avoided physical stress whenever she could, refusing heavy bags, skipping workouts, taking the elevator instead of the stairs, and becoming tense at the first sign of her heart rate rising too quickly. She said she could not stand the sensation of her body “working too hard,” because it made her feel as if she were back in the convoy, trapped in her own skin and unable to protect herself. Even simple errands became carefully managed so she would not have to carry much or push through discomfort. At work, where she sat in a quiet office surrounded by monitors and server logs, she chose tasks that kept her seated and in control of the environment, and she began to dread any assignment that would require moving equipment, staying late, or being on her feet for long periods.

She also started cleaning and organizing repeatedly, describing it less as a habit than as a way to steady herself when her mind felt unsettled. After work she would go home and wipe down counters she had already cleaned, straighten files on her desk, and rearrange drawers until everything looked exact. She knew it looked excessive, but the order gave her a brief sense that something in the world could still be made predictable. If her apartment felt messy, or even if a single item was out of place, she became uneasy and could not rest until she had put it right. The rituals were especially strong on evenings when she had been reminded of the convoy, as though the neatness of her surroundings could compensate for the chaos she could not erase.

Going outside after dark became another boundary she rarely crossed. Nadia described night as the time when the memory felt closest, when streets seemed too open and shadows too similar to the dimness before the blast. She no longer agreed to dinner plans that would run late, turned down invitations from friends, and often left the office before sunset so she would not have to walk to her car in the dark. When work required overtime, she felt caught between embarrassment and dread, and more than once she invented practical excuses to leave early. Over time, colleagues stopped asking her to join them, and she noticed with shame that her social life had narrowed to a few daytime contacts and messages answered from home. She was aware that her world had become smaller, but it still felt safer than testing herself against the dark.

By the time she sought help, the pattern had hardened into a daily way of living. Nadia was exhausted by how much effort it took to avoid strain, keep her apartment in order, and plan every evening around daylight. She came in saying she wanted to sleep without feeling as if the night were waiting for her and to stop organizing her life around the fear that one wrong exertion or one walk after sunset would bring the convoy back in full. What frightened her most was the sense that if she loosened her grip on these routines, the fear would surge and she would not be able to calm herself again.
